plan: In a second-price auction (winner pays second-highest bid), bidding one's true value is a weakly dominant strategy regardless of what other bidders do. This holds true even against strategic, rational opponents—my optimal bid doesn't depend on their beliefs about me, since truthful bidding maximizes expected profit in all cases. With my value at $9, I should bid exactly $9 to ensure I only win when profitable and pay a fair price if I do win.

This is a second-price auction (winner pays second-highest bid). In second-price auctions, the dominant strategy is to bid one's true value, regardless of beliefs about opponents' strategies. Bidding truthfully ensures I win exactly when it's profitable (value > price paid) and never overpay. Since my value is $40, I should bid $40.

This is a second-price (Vickrey) auction: the winner pays the second-highest bid, not their own bid. In such auctions, bidding your true value is a dominant strategy regardless of other bidders' behavior—overbidding risks paying more than the item is worth, while underbidding risks losing profitable opportunities without any benefit. Since my value is $32, I should bid exactly $32 to maximize expected profit, as this strategy is optimal no matter what the other rational bidders do.
